newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada not seen matching a Fed hike.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada not seen matching a Fed hike.

text.p: In a move that would have been unthinkable a few years ago, the Bank of Canada is seen holding interest rates steady in the face of an expected hike in U.S. rates on Tuesday.
Analysts said keeping rates unchanged would be a major test of the central bank's policy of independence from the U.S. Federal Reserve, reflecting Canada's different economic fundamentals.

"I would be extremely surprised if the Bank of Canada did anything. Our situation is dramatically different than the United States. We have very high unemployment and no risk of inflation," said John McCallum, chief economist with Royal Bank of Canada.
Until recently, Canadian interest rate movements mirrored those of the United States, especially when U.S. rates were moving higher.

In 1995, the Bank of Canada was forced to match rising U.S. rates in order to preserve confidence in the Canadian dollar. The central bank has often been required to make such hikes whether or not they were warranted by Canada's domestic economic fundaments.
But falling government deficits and low Canadian inflation have since given the central bank more latitude with rates.
Canada's key bank rate, a benchmark of short-term Canadian rates, is now at 3.25 percent versus a U.S. federal funds rate of 5.25 percent.

Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen told the Senate Banking Committee last week that Canada's improved finances gave the central bank more room to maneuver in response to possible U.S. interest rate rises.
"I think he indicated that the bank, as I expect, will simply do nothing at all," said Tim O'Neill, chief economist with Bank of Montreal. "We're at very different points in the economic cycle."

Unlike the United States, unemployment in Canada is stuck at almost 10 percent and inflationary pressures have been almost non-existent. Economic reports last week confirmed the country's inflation rate was in the lower half of the Bank of Canada's 1.0-3.0 percent target range.

Analysts said the true test of the Bank of Canada's independence would be measured by the performance of the Canadian dollar. If the dollar sold off after a U.S. rate hike, the Bank of Canada would be forced to follow with one or possibly several rate hikes of its own.
But several analysts said that possibility had already been priced into the Canadian dollar, which accounted for the currency's recent decline to its lowest point in more than a year.

A minority of analysts said the Bank of Canada might match a hike in U.S. interest rates. They said Canada's economy had begun showing signs of a pickup in growth, which might warrant a small rise in rates and spare the Canadian dollar the consequences of resisting a Fed hike.
"If they (Bank of Canada) don't go immediately, I think the Canadian dollar will take it on the nose," said Michael Gregory, an economist with Lehman Brothers.
